source: Khieu Borin, Than Soeurn, Preston T.R. and Sato K. 1996. The role of the sugar palm tree (Borassus flabellifer) in livestock based farming systems in Cambodia. In: Sustainable Livestock Production on Local Feed Resources, FAO Regional Office for Asia and the Pacific (RAP Publication), Bangkok.
text: Two farm trials in Takeo province tested sugar-palm-juice-based rations for fattening pigs from about 20kg to market weight. The first trial (72 pigs across 12 farms, Bati district) used a daily ration per pig of about 8kg palm juice, 400g soya beans (156g protein), 500g water spinach, 5g lime, and 5g salt, producing an average daily weight gain of 356g (range 320–417g across farms). The second trial (30 pigs across 15 farms, Samroung district) replaced soya beans with dried freshwater fish: about 6.5kg palm juice, 1kg rice bran, 300g dried fish (110g protein), and 5g salt plus available vegetables, producing a higher average daily gain of 420g (range 220–580g). The higher gain with fish protein is attributed to a better amino-acid balance in fish than in soya beans, and dried fish was also notably cheaper per kg of protein at the time of the trial (soya bean prices in Cambodia ranged from 625 to 1,500 Riels/kg within a single year due to market fluctuation).
